questions.stem: Auditors found the firm's documentation of the design phase {1}, but its record of the subsequent safety inspections was {2} — and it was that gap, rather than any flaw in the engineering, that sank the company's defense.
questions.explanation: The dash clause identifies a "gap" in the inspection record, so the second blank must report a shortfall measured against a standard — the auditors' verdict, wanting. "Exhaustive" and "unimpeachable" would leave no gap at all. The contrastive "but" then forces the first blank to be positive in the same dimension of adequacy: copious, not scant or erratic, both of which would make the two halves agree rather than contrast.

questions.stem: Measured against the exacting standard set by the composer's own recordings, the young virtuoso's phrasing, for all its dazzling speed, was {1}.
questions.explanation: "Measured against" an exacting standard sets up a verdict, and the concessive "for all its dazzling speed" signals that the verdict is unfavorable: the phrasing fell short, so it was wanting or lacking. "Impeccable" reverses the concession, while scant, sparse, and paltry are quantity words — they describe how little of something there is, whereas phrasing fails in quality, not in amount.

questions.stem: The tribunal distinguished sharply between the clerk's {1} misfiling of the ledgers and the executive's {2} destruction of them: only the second act, carried out in full knowledge of the subpoena, drew a criminal charge.
questions.explanation: "In full knowledge of the subpoena" is the classic ground for the second blank: willful means done deliberately with blame attached, which is exactly what converts an act into a crime here. "Negligent" and "unwitting" both concede the absence of that knowledge and so cannot be the distinguishing term. The colon makes the first blank the contrasting case, hence inadvertent; "meticulous" misfiling is incoherent.

questions.stem: Even as a child the future empress was notoriously {1}: she would take no correction from her tutors, doing as she pleased in open defiance of them, and the trait only hardened once she had a court to command.
questions.explanation: The child refuses to be instructed or steered and insists on her own way, which is precisely willful in its headstrong sense. "Intransigent" requires a dispute in which one side refuses to compromise, and "obdurate" describes hardness against pleas or pity; neither is about resisting authority as such. "Pertinacious" praises dogged persistence in a purpose, and "restive" suggests fidgeting under restraint rather than the deliberate defiance described.
